title: int("４２") works -- those are fullwidth Unicode digits, not the ASCII characters they look like
assumption: int() only accepts the ASCII digits 0-9.

input.display: int("\uff14\uff12") == 42  (U+FF14 FULLWIDTH DIGIT FOUR, U+FF12 FULLWIDTH DIGIT TWO)
input.description: User input copy-pasted from a source using fullwidth characters (common in East Asian text contexts, or a sneaky/naughty-string test input), or any other Unicode script's decimal digits (Arabic-Indic, Devanagari, etc.) submitted to a form field.

what_goes_wrong: A validator that checks `s.isdigit()` or `re.fullmatch(r'\d+', s)` and then calls `int(s)` happily accepts fullwidth, Arabic-Indic, Devanagari and other Unicode digits (both checks are Unicode-aware for str), while a check anchored to `[0-9]` rejects the same input that `int()` would accept -- so two layers of the same form can disagree about what a number is.
why: Python's `int()` (and `float()`) accepts any character with the Unicode general category Nd ('decimal digit'), which covers fullwidth forms (U+FF10-FF19), Arabic-Indic, Devanagari and dozens of other scripts' 0-9, and maps each to its decimal value; it also strips any Unicode whitespace around the number. This is documented, deliberate internationalisation in the string-to-number conversion, not in the language's source parser: `x = ４２` in source code is a SyntaxError. Python's regex `\d` is likewise Unicode-aware for str patterns unless you pass `re.ASCII`. And the sets do not line up: `'²'.isdigit()` is True for superscript two, but it is not Nd, so `int('²')` raises.

repros.code:
import re
fullwidth = "\uff14\uff12"  # looks like "42"
print(repr(fullwidth), "->", int(fullwidth))
print("matches [0-9]+:", bool(re.fullmatch(r"[0-9]+", fullwidth)))
print("matches \\d+:", bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d+", fullwidth)), "| with re.ASCII:", bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d+", fullwidth, re.ASCII)))
sup = "\u00b2"  # SUPERSCRIPT TWO
try:
    int(sup)
except ValueError as e:
    print(repr(sup), "isdigit():", sup.isdigit(), "| int() ->", e)
repros.expected_output:
'４２' -> 42
matches [0-9]+: False
matches \d+: True | with re.ASCII: False
'²' isdigit(): True | int() -> invalid literal for int() with base 10: '²'

fix: If you need ASCII digits only, say so explicitly: `s.isascii() and s.isdigit()`, `re.fullmatch(r'[0-9]+', s)` or `re.fullmatch(r'\d+', s, re.ASCII)`, and run `int()` on the same string you validated. If you want to accept other scripts' digits, normalise them deliberately (e.g. `str(int(s))`) before storing or passing the value to systems that only understand ASCII.
